notes.meaning: Isaac still has doubts and asks directly if the young man before him is truly Esau. Jacob does not back down, but boldly repeats his lie to his blind father. A single dishonest choice often forces someone to tell even more lies to protect the secret.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church writers such as Augustine and later Catholic commentators argued that Jacob's words were a prophetic mystery pointing to Christ rather than a malicious lie.

notes.meaning: Isaac asks his son to bring the wild game so he can eat and give his solemn blessing. Jacob serves him the freshly prepared meat and wine, carrying out the disguise completely. In the ancient world, sharing a formal meal together often prepared a father to hand down family leadership.
Isaac asks his son to come close and kiss him. This kiss showed warm fatherly affection and deep love. It also brought Jacob near enough for his father to smell his clothes.

Jacob kisses his father, and Isaac smells Esau's hunting clothes, which smelled of fresh wild plants and open fields. Convinced that the Lord has favored this son, Isaac begins his formal blessing. He compares his son's scent to a fertile field that God has made rich and fruitful.

Isaac prays that God will grant his son the heavy dew from the sky and rich, fertile soil. In a dry country, plentiful dew and good soil meant huge harvests of grain and fresh wine. This prayer asked God to give him abundant food and earthly prosperity.

Isaac blesses his son with leadership over other nations and authority over his own relatives. He adds that anyone who curses him will be cursed, and anyone who blesses him will be blessed. This confirmed God's covenant promise to Abraham, pointing forward to the nation of Israel and the coming of Christ.

Jacob walks out of the room just as his brother Esau returns from hunting. The narrow timing shows how close the deception came to being caught right away. Even through human schemes and close calls, God was guiding who received the blessing.

Esau prepares the wild game he caught and brings it politely to his father. He invites Isaac to sit up, enjoy the meal, and give him the promised blessing. Esau was confident that the rights of the oldest son were finally his to receive.
Isaac is confused and asks the visitor who he is. Esau answers directly that he is his firstborn son. This sudden answer made Isaac realize that someone else had just been in his room.

Isaac shakes violently all over as the truth dawns on him. He explains that he already ate the meal and gave the blessing away, and he insists that the blessing must stay on Jacob. Isaac realized that God had overruled his personal wishes to bless the son God had chosen.

Esau cries out with a loud and bitter shout of grief when he hears his father's words. He begs Isaac to give him a blessing too. Esau was heartbroken over losing his family honor and wealth, even though he had earlier given away his birthright very cheaply.

differ.view: Many Methodists teach that Isaac could not change his mind because the blessing was already settled, so Esau was rejected from the covenant blessing rather than from eternal salvation.

notes.meaning: Isaac tells Esau that his brother came with deceit and took away the blessing. A formal patriarchal blessing was seen as a binding gift from God that could not be revoked. Even though Jacob used trickery, Isaac knew the spoken words had to stand.

Esau complains that Jacob's name fits him perfectly, since it sounds like a word for a deceiver or someone who trips others up. He claims Jacob cheated him twice, first out of his birthright and now out of his blessing. Esau blamed his brother for taking the birthright, conveniently ignoring that he had willingly traded it away for a bowl of stew.

Isaac explains to Esau that he has already made Jacob master over the family and sustained him with grain and wine. He feels there is no major covenant blessing left to hand out. Isaac spoke as God's prophet, knowing he could not make promises on his own authority.

Esau weeps aloud and asks his father if he really has only one blessing to give. He desperately pleads for any kind of favor his father can grant him. He cared deeply about the comfort and honor he had lost, even though he had not valued God's covenant earlier in life.

Isaac describes the kind of land where Esau and his family will make their home. Instead of the fertile soil given to Jacob, Esau's land would be rough and dry. Even in material things, Esau was left with a much harsher homeland than his brother.

differ.view: Read the Hebrew words as a genuine promise that Esau would share in the fat of the earth and the dew of heaven, though without the covenant blessing.
Translate the Hebrew words as 'away from' the richness of the earth, predicting that Esau's descendants would live in a barren, rocky desert.

notes.meaning: Isaac tells Esau that he will live by the sword and serve his younger brother. However, he also promises that when Esau grows restless and rebels, he will eventually break Jacob's yoke off his neck. This was fulfilled centuries later when the Edomites served Israel under King David and then successfully revolted under King Jehoram.

Esau holds a deep, bitter grudge against Jacob because of the lost blessing. He plans to wait until their father dies and the days of mourning end, and then murder his brother. Unchecked jealousy and anger can quickly grow into violent hatred.

Someone warns Rebekah that Esau is planning to kill Jacob. She quickly sends for her younger son to tell him that Esau is comforting himself with thoughts of murder. Rebekah realizes that her scheme has put her favorite son in deadly danger.

Rebekah tells Jacob to obey her voice right away and run for his life. She instructs him to flee to her brother Laban in the distant land of Haran. Sin often drives people away from the very home and safety they were trying to protect.

Rebekah tells Jacob to stay with Laban for just a little while until Esau's anger cools down. She hoped the separation would be brief and easy. In reality, Jacob remained away for twenty long years, showing how badly her expectations failed.

Rebekah asks why she should have to lose both of her sons in a single day. She knew that if Esau killed Jacob, family justice or God's judgment would require Esau to be put to death too. Her scheming brought great anxiety and pain instead of peaceful security.

Rebekah complains to Isaac about Esau's local Hittite wives, saying her life would be miserable if Jacob married a local woman too. She used a real household concern to convince Isaac to send Jacob away safely. Jacob left home as a lonely traveler, showing that dishonesty always carries painful consequences.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars view this verse as coming from a separate ancient source where Jacob is sent away simply to find a wife, without any mention of Esau's death threats.
